A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same spatiotemporal engression work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original closed-loop simulations, forecasting experiments on six epidemic datasets, and analyses of calibration, noise propagation, and spatial importance.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds component ablations with numerical results in Tables 14–16 and associated ranking and calibration plots.

M1.justification: Equation (1) corrects the spatial-distance formula from cos(longitude_i)cos(longitude_j) to cos(latitude_i)cos(latitude_j), refining the specified graph and spatial-weight construction. The MVEN, GCEN, and STEN architectures and Algorithms 1–4 otherwise remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish an implementation change or rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions use Japan and China tuberculosis, USA influenza-like illness, Belgium COVID-19, Colombia dengue, and Hungary chickenpox data, alongside the same simulation setting and Guainia motivating example. The new ablations reuse existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 1 adds an evaluated DeepAR median and probabilistic cloud to the Guainia comparison, which previously showed ARIMA, ARNN, LSTM, and MVEN. The twelve external baselines in the main forecasting comparisons remain unchanged; v2 additionally introduces the component controls assessed under E4.

E3.justification: Section 8 adds controlled experiments with identical hyperparameters, moving noise to the output or replacing energy-score training with MSE averaged over two sampled trajectories. The original temporal splits, forecast horizons, training budgets, and evaluation ensemble sizes remain unchanged. The added baseline configuration paragraph primarily supplies previously undocumented settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic pre-additive versus post-additive noise and energy-score versus MSE ablations for all three architectures across the retained datasets and horizons. Tables 14–16, the MCB comparisons in Figure 12, and PIT plots in Figure 14 substantially extend v1's toy loss illustration and existing explainability analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over 50 forecast-generation evaluations of a trained model, use 200 simulation trials, and employ MCB comparisons. The added ablations follow the existing reporting practices; they do not establish increased training repetitions, new seed reporting, or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The existing benchmark, coverage, and runtime values are retained after renumbering. Tables 14–16 add extensive component results: for Japan's six-month horizon, GCEN CRPS is 4.23, versus 5.90 for GCEN-Post and 6.11 for GCEN-MSE. New aggregate rankings and calibration findings accompany these results, and Figure 1 adds DeepAR and revises the displayed MVEN fit.

T1.justification: Equation (1) corrects the Haversine distance definition by replacing longitude cosine factors with latitude factors. The formal ergodicity definitions, assumptions A1–A6, theorems, corollaries, and Appendix A proofs otherwise retain their mathematical substance; expanded practical remarks mainly concern interpretation.

C1.justification: The new contribution list explicitly claims first pre-additive, energy-score spatiotemporal frameworks and first stationarity analysis for this model class, and presents existing architectures as special cases. The conclusion narrows the stated theoretical contribution to closed-loop versions. The principal forecasting contributions and abstract performance claims remain stable.

C2.justification: Sections 3 and 9 newly qualify extrapolation benefits because classical engression's monotonicity assumptions fail in realistic spatiotemporal settings. Section 5.2 distinguishes idealized closed-loop theory from finite-sample forecasting without hidden-state noise. v2 also adds substantive interpretations of ablation-induced distribution collapse, model-selection tradeoffs, and recalibration as a response to overconfidence.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies library-default configurations for several baselines, original-paper settings for others, validation tuning of LSTM, and common input/output windows. Section 8 documents the ablation construction and MSE computation. A package-documentation link is added; the existing code repository, hardware descriptions, and proposed-model search ranges are retained.

R1.justification: v2 positions engression alongside mixture density networks and normalizing flows, adding Bishop and Papamakarios citations. It also adds Jaeger for hidden-state perturbations and Hu for spatial extrapolation, while removing several introductory forecasting references. The Kipf citation's publication update refers to the same work and does not constitute a new research connection.

P1.justification: Focused revisions rewrite the background and theoretical implications, expand the motivating explanation, shorten redundant STEN exposition, and add an explicit contribution list. A dedicated ablation section, broader-impact statement, and acknowledgements are introduced, while the overall methodological narrative and Appendix A–G organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adopts substantially different typography and page layout, expands Figure 1 to three panels, moves the architecture diagram from v1 Figure 13 to main-text Figure 2, and adds ablation tables and plots. It removes v1's split schematic, historical-series figure, and adjacency heatmaps, and rearranges existing appendix tables and figures.

improvement.justification: The systematic component controls in Section 8 and Tables 14–16 address an important gap in v1: empirical support for the central noise-placement and loss-function choices relied largely on motivation and a toy illustration. Clearer limits on theoretical applicability, the distance-formula correction, and baseline configuration disclosure further strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh the loss of descriptive figures and some overstated new interpretations, particularly claims of spatial-model statistical superiority despite overlapping intervals in Figure 12.
